theory.text: Part 3
A step-by-step self-study guide
Understand abstract questions • Develop ideas • Compare and evaluate • Support opinions • Practise full discussions

rows: GUIDE PURPOSE  This guide focuses on IELTS Speaking Part 3: the discussion that follows Part 2. It helps you move beyond personal description and explain opinions, causes, consequences, comparisons and possible solutions.

theory.text: The guide is designed for independent study. Work through the theory, practise one small skill at a time, plan answers with keywords, and then complete the full discussion sets. The answer key at the end contains sample responses and planning notes.
Important: sample answers are models of development, not scripts to memorise. Use examples that are truthful or plausible for you, and adapt the language to your own level.
Your learning route
Session 1 — Read the theory and speak the worked examples aloud. Notice how each answer develops one main idea.
Session 2 — Complete E1–E10. Focus on the skill named in each exercise rather than trying to sound advanced.
Session 3 — Complete P1–P10 with keywords only. Do not write full paragraphs during planning.
Session 4 — Record yourself answering one full practice set. Listen for relevance, development, pauses and repeated vocabulary.
Session 5 — Compare your recording with the model answers, identify one weakness, and repeat the set.

rows: PRACTICE TARGET  Part 3 normally lasts about 4–5 minutes. There is no fixed number of sentences required for every answer. Aim to answer directly, develop the idea sufficiently, and stop before the answer becomes repetitive or unrelated.

theory.text: Part 1 – Theory
1. Understand the purpose of Part 3

IELTS Speaking Part 3 is a two-way discussion with the examiner, usually lasting around 4–5 minutes. The questions are connected to the broad theme of Part 2, but they generally ask you to discuss wider issues rather than retell your own story. You may be asked about society, changes over time, causes, effects, differences between groups, future trends or possible solutions.

For example, if your Part 2 topic was a useful skill, Part 3 might ask why some skills are more important today, how schools should teach practical skills, or whether technology makes people less independent.

rows: KEY DISTINCTION  Part 1 often asks about your own familiar life; Part 2 asks you to give a long turn on a cue-card topic; Part 3 asks you to discuss and reason about broader questions. Personal examples can still help in Part 3, but they should support the answer rather than replace the wider discussion.

theory.text: 2. Identify what the question is asking
Before answering, recognise the question type. The wording often tells you which thinking move to make.

rows: Do you think…? Is it important…? Should…?
State your position and explain why.
Give one or two causes and explain the link.
Name a benefit or drawback and show its effect.
How is X different from Y? Do young and older people…?
Choose a clear comparison point; avoid treating everyone as identical.
How has X changed? Was it different in the past?
Describe the change and explain why it happened.
How might X change? Will people… in the future?
Make a cautious prediction and give a reason.
How can this problem be solved? Who should…?
Suggest realistic actions and identify who can take them.
Why does X matter? What makes something successful?
Define the idea briefly, then discuss its importance or criteria.

theory.text: 3. Use a flexible answer structure: Answer → Explain → Example → Qualification

A useful structure is A–E–E–Q: Answer the question, Explain your reasoning, give an Example or consequence, and add a Qualification when it makes the answer more accurate. You do not need all four steps every time. Use the structure as a mental guide, not a fixed script.
WORKED EXAMPLE • Question: “Why do some people prefer shopping online?”

Model answer: “I think convenience is the main reason. People can compare prices and order things without travelling to a shop, which is especially useful when they have busy schedules. For example, a student can buy stationery late in the evening instead of trying to fit a shopping trip into the day. However, some people still prefer physical shops when they need to check the quality or size of an item.”

HOW THE THEORY APPLIES • Answer: convenience. Explanation: it saves travel and makes comparison easier. Example: a student shopping late. Qualification: physical shops remain useful for checking products. Each sentence adds a different piece of reasoning.
4. Develop an idea instead of listing points

A common weakness is giving several short claims without explaining any of them: “It is useful. It saves time. It is cheap. It is popular.” A stronger answer develops one main point by showing how or why it matters. If you have time, add a second point that is genuinely different.

Try the chain: claim → mechanism → result. For instance, “Public transport can reduce traffic” is a claim. “If buses and trains are reliable, some commuters may leave their cars at home” explains the mechanism. “That can reduce congestion and make travel times more predictable” shows a result.

rows: SELF-CHECK  After making a claim, ask yourself: “Why?”, “How does that happen?”, “Can I give a realistic example?”, or “Does this apply in every situation?” One good follow-up is usually more valuable than another unsupported claim.

theory.text: 5. Make examples specific but not overlong

An example can be personal, hypothetical or based on a familiar situation. You do not need statistics or expert facts. A short, concrete example often makes an abstract point easier to understand. Avoid inventing precise figures when you do not know them, and do not let the example take over the answer.
WEAK • “Technology is useful because it is good for people.”
STRONGER • “Technology can make learning more flexible. For example, someone who works during the day can watch a recorded lesson in the evening and review difficult sections at their own pace.”
6. Compare groups without overgeneralising

Questions may compare children and adults, younger and older people, urban and rural communities, or the past and present. Identify the dimension of comparison—such as access, priorities, habits or responsibilities—and explain it. Avoid absolute statements such as “all young people” or “older people never”. Useful qualifiers include many, some, often, tend to, may and in some circumstances.
WORKED EXAMPLE • Question: “Do young and older people use technology differently?”

Model answer: “They can, partly because they may use it for different purposes. Younger people often use digital tools for study and socialising, while some older adults may focus more on communication with family or practical services. Of course, these are broad tendencies rather than rules, because experience and personal interests matter too.”
7. Discuss change over time

For past-versus-present questions, name the change, compare the two periods, and explain a possible cause or consequence. Useful language includes used to, whereas, compared with, has become more common, over the last few decades and one reason may be.
WORKED EXAMPLE • Question: “How has the way people learn changed?”

Model answer: “Learning has become more flexible. In the past, many learners depended mainly on classroom lessons and printed materials, whereas now they can also use online courses and recorded videos. Wider internet access is one reason for this change, although face-to-face teaching is still valuable for discussion and feedback.”
8. Make predictions carefully

Future questions invite a reasoned possibility, not a guaranteed forecast. State what may happen, explain the trend behind your prediction, and acknowledge uncertainty if relevant. Phrases such as may, might, is likely to, could, if this trend continues and it depends on help you avoid sounding overconfident.
WORKED EXAMPLE • Question: “Will people read fewer printed books in the future?”

Model answer: “They may read fewer printed books for convenience, because digital books are easy to carry and can be downloaded immediately. However, I do not think printed books will disappear completely. Some readers enjoy the physical experience, and printed materials may remain popular for collecting or studying.”
9. Discuss problems, solutions and responsibility

When asked how to solve a problem, avoid saying only that people should “raise awareness”. Identify a concrete action, the person or organisation responsible, and the likely effect. Solutions can involve individuals, schools, employers, communities or governments. A balanced answer may explain why one group cannot solve the problem alone.
WORKED EXAMPLE • Question: “How can cities encourage people to use public transport?”

Model answer: “Local authorities could make public transport more reliable and affordable. If buses arrive regularly and connect residential areas with workplaces, people have a stronger reason to use them instead of driving. Employers could also support this by offering travel benefits. Public campaigns may help, but convenience is likely to matter more than slogans.”
10. Use grammar to express relationships between ideas

Part 3 gives you opportunities to use a range of sentence structures naturally. You do not need to force complicated grammar into every answer. Choose structures that express the relationship you mean.
Cause: because, since, one reason is that…
Result: therefore, as a result, which means that…
Contrast: whereas, while, however, on the other hand…
Condition: if…, unless…, provided that…
Concession: although…, even though…, it is true that…
Possibility: may, might, could, is likely to…
Comparison: compared with…, unlike…, in contrast to…

WORKED EXAMPLE • “Online learning is convenient, although it may be less effective for students who need immediate feedback. If teachers combine recorded lessons with live discussion, learners can benefit from both flexibility and interaction.”
11. Vocabulary: precision is better than decoration

A good answer uses words that express the intended idea precisely. You can often improve a response by replacing a vague word with a more specific one: good → effective / beneficial; bad → harmful / inconvenient; a lot of people → many people / a large proportion of people (only when appropriate); make better → improve / strengthen. Do not use a word merely because it sounds academic.
Useful topic-neutral phrases:
One major factor is…
This is largely because…
A possible consequence is…
The main difference is that…
This tends to be more common among…
That said, it does not necessarily mean that…
It depends on factors such as…
A practical way to address this would be to…
If the trend continues, we may see…
There are exceptions, of course.
12. Fluency, pronunciation and recovery

Fluency does not mean speaking as fast as possible. It means maintaining a reasonably natural flow, connecting ideas and recovering when you need a moment to think. Pause briefly to organise your answer rather than filling every gap with “um”, “like” or repeated phrases. Stress the key words in a sentence and make the relationships between ideas audible.

If you do not know a fact, do not pretend to know it. Give a reasoned general answer, state that it can vary, or use a hypothetical example. If you lose your point, return to the question and summarise your main idea.

rows: RECOVERY PHRASES  “I would say the main reason is…” • “It probably depends on…” • “One example that comes to mind is…” • “I have not thought about that before, but I would imagine…” Use these naturally; do not use them as memorised openings for every answer.

theory.text: 13. Common mistakes to avoid
Answering a different question because it is easier to discuss.
Giving a personal story without linking it to the wider issue.
Listing three or four reasons without explaining any of them.
Using absolute claims about whole age groups or societies.
Making unsupported claims with precise statistics.
Forcing idioms, rare vocabulary or long complex sentences.
Repeating the same point in different words.
Speaking for too long after the question has already been answered.
Treating a prediction as a certain fact.
Memorising model answers and struggling when the wording changes.
14. What the examiner assesses

IELTS Speaking is assessed through four criteria: fluency and coherence, lexical resource, grammatical range and accuracy, and pronunciation. Part 3 is not a test of specialist knowledge. The examiner is interested in how clearly and effectively you express and develop ideas in English. A simple, relevant answer with clear reasoning can be stronger than an elaborate answer full of vague claims.

rows: Did I answer directly? Were my ideas connected and developed without unnecessary repetition?
Did I choose precise words and paraphrase when needed? Did I avoid repeating the same vague words?
Did I use a mix of simple and complex sentences that I could control?
Could a listener follow my message easily? Were key words and sentence stress clear?

theory.text: 15. A practical answer checklist
☐ I responded to the exact question in my first sentence.
☐ I explained at least one reason, mechanism or consequence.
☐ I used a relevant example or comparison when it helped.
☐ I qualified my point when a generalisation would be too strong.
☐ I used linking language naturally and did not overuse fillers.
☐ I stopped when the idea was sufficiently developed.

guide.text: Part 3 – Planning Guide
A. The 10-second mental plan
You normally do not receive a separate preparation minute for Part 3 questions, so practise organising a response quickly. Use a short mental sequence:
QUESTION — What exactly is being asked: why, whether, how, compare, predict or solve?
POSITION — What is my direct answer or main claim?
DEVELOP — What is the strongest reason, mechanism or consequence?
SUPPORT — What example, comparison or qualification will make it clearer?
STOP — Have I answered the question without repeating myself?
B. Planning sheet
Use this template when practising. Fill it with short words or phrases, not a complete script.

rows: One sentence I should avoid repeating

guide.text: C. How much should I say?

There is no fixed answer length that guarantees a particular band score. As a practice starting point, many Part 3 answers can be developed in roughly 3–5 connected sentences, but some questions need less and some need more. Prioritise the quality of development, not a sentence count.
If the answer is too short: add a reason or explain how the situation works.
If the answer is repetitive: give one specific example or move to a relevant qualification.
If the answer is drifting: return to the key wording of the question.
If you cannot think of a personal example: use a realistic general or hypothetical example.
D. Planning tasks P1–P10
P1. Education
Question: Why is it important for schools to teach practical skills?
Keywords: independence; everyday decisions; money/time; prepare for adult life; academics still matter.
P2. Technology
Question: Has technology improved communication?
Keywords: instant contact; distance; video calls; distraction/misunderstanding; depends on use.
P3. Work
Question: What makes a job satisfying?
Keywords: meaningful tasks; fair pay; supportive team; growth; priorities differ.
P4. Environment
Question: How can individuals help protect the environment?
Keywords: reduce waste; transport choices; habits; infrastructure matters; not individual responsibility alone.
P5. Cities
Question: Why do people move to large cities?
Keywords: jobs; education; services; opportunity; cost/crowding trade-off.
P6. Family and society
Question: Have family relationships changed?
Keywords: smaller households/mobility; technology keeps contact; less shared time; variation by family.
P7. Health and lifestyle
Question: Why do some people find it difficult to exercise regularly?
Keywords: time; tiredness; access; routine; small realistic changes.
P8. Culture
Question: Should traditional customs be preserved?
Keywords: identity; shared history; community; adapt rather than freeze; harmful practices may change.
P9. Consumer behaviour
Question: Why do people buy things they do not really need?
Keywords: advertising; emotion; social pressure; convenience; budget/awareness.
P10. Future
Question: How might AI change the workplace?
Keywords: automate routine tasks; support decisions; new skills; job transitions; human judgement.
E. Useful language bank

rows: I would argue that… / In general, I think… / To a large extent, yes.
One important reason is… / This is partly because… / The main factor may be…
As a result… / This can lead to… / That means…
For example… / A common example would be… / Imagine a student who…
Compared with… / Whereas… / One key difference is…
In many cases… / This is not always true, though… / It depends on…
In the past… whereas now… / This has become more common because…
It may be that… / If the trend continues… / I would expect…
One practical step would be… / Schools or local authorities could…
I have not considered that before, but… / The first thing that comes to mind is…

small.text: Part 2 – Small Exercises
Complete these short activities before attempting full discussions. Speak your answers aloud whenever possible. For planning exercises, write keywords rather than complete sentences.
E1. Identify the question type
For each question, label it as opinion, cause, comparison, change, prediction, solution or advantage/disadvantage.
Why do some people prefer living in large cities?
How has communication changed in the last twenty years?
Should schools teach students how to manage money?
What might workplaces look like in the future?
How can communities reduce food waste?
Are there any disadvantages to studying online?
E2. Answer the question directly
Write or say one opening sentence that clearly answers each question. Do not explain yet.
Why do people enjoy travelling?
Is it important for children to learn teamwork?
Do you think public parks are necessary in cities?
Will technology replace some traditional jobs?
E3. Build a reason chain
For each claim, add (a) why/how it happens and (b) one result. Avoid adding unrelated reasons.
Public libraries are still useful.
Learning a second language can benefit young people.
Flexible working can improve people's lives.
Too much packaging creates environmental problems.
E4. Add a specific example
Add one short, realistic example to each statement. Keep the example to one or two sentences.
Online resources make learning more flexible.
Sports can teach people to cooperate.
Small local businesses can strengthen a community.
Planning ahead can reduce stress.
E5. Compare without overgeneralising
Complete each comparison with one clear difference and one qualifier such as often, may, some or tend to.
Children and adults may learn differently because…
Living in a city can be different from living in the countryside because…
People today communicate differently from people in the past because…
Working from home differs from working in an office because…
E6. Discuss change over time
For each topic, identify one change and one possible reason for it. Then speak for 20–30 seconds.
How people shop
How students access information
How families spend time together
How people keep in touch with friends
E7. Make a careful prediction
Give one prediction, one reason and one qualification. Use may, might, could or is likely to where appropriate.
Will public transport become more popular?
How might education change in the next twenty years?
Will people spend more or less time outdoors?
How could artificial intelligence affect everyday work?
E8. Suggest a realistic solution
For each problem, identify who could act, what they could do, and how it might help.
Young people do not get enough sleep.
Some neighbourhoods have too much litter.
Students feel stressed before examinations.
People waste food at home.
E9. Add a qualification or counterpoint
Improve each claim by explaining when it may not apply or by acknowledging a different view.
Online learning is better than classroom learning.
People should always choose a high-paying job.
Technology makes communication easier.
Cities are better places for young people.
E10. Recover when you need thinking time
Practise beginning with a natural thinking phrase, then give a direct answer and one reason. Do not repeat the phrase mechanically.
Why do some people avoid public speaking?
What makes a good teacher?
Should people spend less time on social media?
Why are some traditions still important?

full.text: Part 4 – Full Practice

Each set contains questions linked by a broad theme. Answer each question as if you were speaking to an examiner. Do not prepare full scripts in advance. For a realistic practice round, ask another person to read the questions in order, or record yourself and leave only a short pause before each answer.
Suggested routine: answer all questions in a set; listen once for relevance and development; listen again for vocabulary, grammar and pronunciation; then repeat the two weakest answers.
F1. Education and learning
Why should schools teach skills that are not directly related to academic subjects?
Do students learn better from teachers or from digital resources?
How has access to education changed in recent decades?
Should adults continue learning after they finish formal education?
After answering, rate yourself from 1–5 for relevance, development, vocabulary, grammar and ease of understanding. Record one sentence you want to improve.
F2. Technology and communication
Why do people use messaging apps instead of making phone calls?
Has technology made relationships stronger or weaker?
Do older and younger people use technology for different reasons?
How might communication technology change in the future?
After answering, rate yourself from 1–5 for relevance, development, vocabulary, grammar and ease of understanding. Record one sentence you want to improve.
F3. Work and careers
What factors are important when people choose a career?
Is job satisfaction more important than a high salary?
How has working life changed compared with the past?
Which responsibilities should employers have towards their workers?
After answering, rate yourself from 1–5 for relevance, development, vocabulary, grammar and ease of understanding. Record one sentence you want to improve.
F4. Environment and communities
Why is it difficult for people to change environmentally harmful habits?
What can governments do to encourage people to recycle?
Should environmental protection be the responsibility of individuals or organisations?
Do you think people will live more sustainably in the future?
After answering, rate yourself from 1–5 for relevance, development, vocabulary, grammar and ease of understanding. Record one sentence you want to improve.
F5. Cities and the countryside
Why do many people move from rural areas to cities?
What are the main disadvantages of living in a large city?
How can cities become better places for families?
Do you think more people will choose to live outside cities in the future?
After answering, rate yourself from 1–5 for relevance, development, vocabulary, grammar and ease of understanding. Record one sentence you want to improve.
F6. Family and relationships
How important is it for families to spend time together?
How have family roles changed in recent years?
Do children benefit from spending time with people of different ages?
How can people maintain relationships when they live far apart?
After answering, rate yourself from 1–5 for relevance, development, vocabulary, grammar and ease of understanding. Record one sentence you want to improve.
F7. Health and lifestyle
Why do some people find it difficult to maintain healthy habits?
Should schools be responsible for teaching children about health?
How does modern life affect people's free time and stress levels?
What could communities do to help people become more active?
After answering, rate yourself from 1–5 for relevance, development, vocabulary, grammar and ease of understanding. Record one sentence you want to improve.
F8. Culture and traditions
Why are traditions important to some communities?
Should young people be encouraged to learn about local history?
Can traditions change while still keeping their meaning?
How might globalisation affect local cultures in the future?
After answering, rate yourself from 1–5 for relevance, development, vocabulary, grammar and ease of understanding. Record one sentence you want to improve.
F9. Shopping and consumer behaviour
Why do people sometimes buy things they do not need?
How does advertising influence people's decisions?
Are local shops still important when online shopping is available?
What could people do to make more responsible purchasing decisions?
After answering, rate yourself from 1–5 for relevance, development, vocabulary, grammar and ease of understanding. Record one sentence you want to improve.
F10. Media and information
Why do people follow news about events happening far away?
How can people decide whether information online is reliable?
Do you think social media has changed public discussion?
Should schools teach students how to evaluate online information?
After answering, rate yourself from 1–5 for relevance, development, vocabulary, grammar and ease of understanding. Record one sentence you want to improve.
F11. Travel and tourism
Why do people want to visit places that are different from their homes?
What benefits can tourism bring to local communities?
What problems can large numbers of tourists cause?
How might people's travel habits change in the future?
After answering, rate yourself from 1–5 for relevance, development, vocabulary, grammar and ease of understanding. Record one sentence you want to improve.
F12. Artificial intelligence and the future
Why are people interested in using artificial intelligence?
What kinds of tasks should still require human judgement?
How can schools prepare students for changes in the workplace?
Do you think technology will create as many jobs as it replaces?
After answering, rate yourself from 1–5 for relevance, development, vocabulary, grammar and ease of understanding. Record one sentence you want to improve.

review.text: Part 5 – Complete Answer Key

The answers below are examples, not the only correct responses. For open-ended speaking tasks, compare your reasoning and development rather than trying to reproduce the exact wording. Your own examples may be different.
E1. Identify the question type
1. Reasons / causes.
2. Change over time.
3. Opinion / recommendation.
4. Prediction.
5. Solution.
6. Disadvantages.
E2. Answer the question directly
1. “People often enjoy travelling because it lets them experience new places and take a break from their usual routines.”
2. “Yes, I think teamwork is important because children need to learn how to cooperate and solve problems with others.”
3. “Yes. Public parks give residents space to relax and exercise, especially when they do not have a garden.”
4. “Yes, I think technology will replace some routine tasks, although many jobs will still need human judgement and communication.”
E3. Build a reason chain
1. Libraries provide free access to books, study space and sometimes digital resources; this helps people who cannot afford every resource themselves.
2. A second language can help young people communicate across cultures; this may broaden their study or career opportunities.
3. Flexible working can reduce commuting time; people may then have more time for family or rest, although boundaries between work and home can become less clear.
4. Excess packaging creates more rubbish; if it is difficult to recycle, more of it may end up in landfill or the natural environment.
E4. Add a specific example
1. “A student who misses a lesson can watch a recorded explanation later and pause it when a concept is difficult.”
2. “In a team sport, players have to pass the ball and coordinate their movements rather than trying to win individually.”
3. “A neighbourhood shop may know its regular customers and provide products that suit local needs.”
4. “Someone who prepares a weekly study schedule can divide a large assignment into smaller tasks instead of doing everything the night before.”
E5. Compare without overgeneralising
1. “Children may learn well through games and repetition, whereas adults often connect new information to previous experience, although individual learning styles vary.”
2. “Cities usually offer more public services and job options, while rural areas may provide more space and a quieter environment; this depends on the particular location.”
3. “People today can contact others instantly through digital tools, whereas communication in the past often took longer, although face-to-face conversation has remained important.”
4. “Working from home can offer flexibility, while an office may make collaboration easier; the better option depends on the job and the worker.”
E6. Discuss change over time
1. Online shopping and digital payments have become more common, partly because they save time and make it easier to compare products.
2. Students can now access online courses, videos and digital libraries, partly due to wider internet access.
3. Some families use digital entertainment more often, which can reduce shared activities unless they deliberately make time together.
4. Messaging and video calls make it easier to keep in touch over long distances, although people may still value in-person meetings.
E7. Make a careful prediction
1. “Public transport may become more popular if services become reliable and affordable, especially in cities where traffic is a serious problem.”
2. “Education could become more personalised through digital tools, although teachers will probably remain important for feedback and social learning.”
3. “Some people may spend less time outdoors because of screen-based entertainment, but access to parks and community activities could encourage outdoor habits.”
4. “AI is likely to automate some repetitive tasks and support decision-making, but the impact will depend on how workplaces use it and train staff.”
E8. Suggest a realistic solution
1. Schools and families can help teenagers build regular sleep routines and reduce late-night screen use; a consistent schedule may make adequate sleep easier.
2. Residents can use clearly placed bins and community clean-up days, while local authorities need to collect rubbish regularly.
3. Teachers can help students plan revision in smaller stages, and schools can communicate expectations clearly to reduce avoidable last-minute pressure.
4. Households can plan meals, store food properly and freeze leftovers; shops can also improve stock planning and offer appropriate discounts.
E9. Add a qualification or counterpoint
1. “Online learning is more flexible, but classroom learning may be better for students who need immediate interaction or a structured environment.”
2. “A high salary matters because people need financial security, but it should not be the only factor; working conditions and personal interests also affect long-term satisfaction.”
3. “Technology makes it easier to contact people quickly, although constant notifications can distract us and online messages sometimes lack emotional nuance.”
4. “Cities may offer more study and career opportunities, but smaller communities can provide a stronger sense of familiarity and lower living costs in some cases.”
E10. Recover when you need thinking time
1. “I think people may avoid public speaking because they are afraid of making mistakes or being judged. Practice can help them feel more confident.”
2. “A good teacher needs clear subject knowledge and the ability to explain ideas patiently. They should also notice when students are struggling.”
3. “I think many people would benefit from spending less time on social media, particularly if it affects sleep or concentration. However, it can also help people stay connected.”
4. “Traditions can give people a sense of identity and connection with previous generations. I think they remain important when communities can adapt them to modern life.”

Full practice: model answers
F1. Education and learning

Q1. Schools should teach practical skills because academic knowledge alone does not prepare students for every everyday decision. For example, basic financial planning can help young adults manage a budget and avoid unnecessary debt. These skills can be taught alongside academic subjects rather than replacing them.

Q2. I think both can be effective for different reasons. Teachers can respond to questions and notice confusion, while digital resources let students review material at their own pace. A combination is often useful, provided students receive guidance about which resources are reliable.

Q3. Access has become more flexible in many places. Students can use online lessons, digital libraries and recorded lectures, whereas access in the past often depended more heavily on local schools and printed resources. However, internet access and educational quality still vary.

Q4. Yes, because knowledge and working practices continue to change. Adults may need to learn new digital tools or develop communication skills as their jobs change. Continuing education can also be personally rewarding, although people need time and affordable opportunities to take part.
F2. Technology and communication

Q1. Messaging is quick and convenient, and people can reply when they have time rather than arranging a call. It is also useful for sharing links, photos or practical details. However, a phone call may be better when a conversation is emotional or complicated.

Q2. I think it has done both. It helps friends and relatives stay in touch across long distances, especially through video calls. On the other hand, online interaction can become superficial if people are distracted or rarely meet in person, so the effect depends on how technology is used.

Q3. They may do so, partly because of different experience and needs. Younger people often use digital services for study, entertainment and social networking, while some older users may prioritise messaging family or accessing practical services. These are only general tendencies, not rules for every person.

Q4. Communication may become more immediate and personalised as tools improve. For example, translation features could make it easier for people who speak different languages to communicate. Still, privacy, misinformation and unequal access are likely to remain important concerns.
F3. Work and careers

Q1. People often consider salary, stability, personal interests and opportunities to develop. The importance of each factor varies with a person's situation; for example, someone supporting a family may prioritise reliable income, while a recent graduate may value learning opportunities.

Q2. I would not say one is always more important. A fair salary is essential for financial security, but a high income may not compensate for unsafe conditions or constant stress. Ideally, people find a balance between reasonable pay, meaningful work and a manageable schedule.

Q3. Technology has changed how many people communicate and complete tasks. Some can work remotely or collaborate with colleagues in other countries, while routine tasks may be automated. However, not every job can be done online, and some workers face new pressure to learn unfamiliar tools.

Q4. Employers should provide a safe workplace, fair treatment and clear expectations. They can also support training and reasonable work-life boundaries. These responsibilities can benefit workers and the organisation, because people are more likely to perform well when they feel respected.
F4. Environment and communities

Q1. People may find change difficult when the convenient option is also the harmful one. For example, someone may use a car because public transport is unreliable, even if they want to reduce emissions. Habits, cost and access all affect whether people can change their behaviour.

Q2. Governments can make recycling easier by providing clear instructions, accessible collection points and consistent waste services. They can also encourage businesses to reduce unnecessary packaging. Information is useful, but people are more likely to recycle when the system is convenient.

Q3. Both have responsibilities. Individuals can reduce waste and make thoughtful choices, but organisations and governments control many larger systems, such as public transport, energy and product packaging. Cooperation is more realistic than expecting one group to solve everything.

Q4. People may adopt more sustainable habits if low-waste products and public transport become easier to use. However, progress will depend on infrastructure, affordability and policy, not just personal motivation. I would expect gradual change rather than a complete transformation everywhere.
F5. Cities and the countryside

Q1. Large cities often offer a wider range of jobs, universities, hospitals and public services. People may move there to study or improve their career prospects. However, high housing costs can make city life difficult, so the benefits depend on someone's priorities and income.

Q2. The main disadvantages are often congestion, expensive housing and noise. These can increase stress and make daily journeys longer. Some people also feel less connected to their neighbours, although this varies a great deal between neighbourhoods.

Q3. Cities can support families by providing safe parks, affordable childcare, reliable public transport and accessible healthcare. These services make daily life easier, especially for parents who work. Good housing and safe streets are equally important.

Q4. Some people may move to smaller towns if remote work remains practical and local services improve. They could enjoy more space and lower costs. Still, people who need specialised jobs or universities may continue to prefer large cities.
F6. Family and relationships

Q1. Spending time together helps family members share experiences and understand one another's concerns. It does not necessarily require expensive activities; eating together or taking a walk can create opportunities to talk. The important thing is giving each other attention.

Q2. Family roles have become more varied in many societies. More women work outside the home, and some families share childcare and household tasks more equally. However, changes differ by culture, income and individual circumstances, so there is no single pattern.

Q3. Yes, it can help children understand different perspectives and learn patience. Older relatives may share experiences, while children can introduce them to new interests or technology. These relationships work best when people treat one another respectfully and have opportunities to interact.

Q4. Digital tools make regular contact easier through messages and video calls. People can also plan visits and share important events online. Nevertheless, online contact may not replace physical presence entirely, so making time for visits can still matter.
F7. Health and lifestyle

Q1. Busy schedules, tiredness, cost and limited access to facilities can make healthy habits difficult. People may know that exercise is beneficial but struggle to fit it around work or study. Small, realistic routines are often easier to maintain than sudden, demanding changes.

Q2. Schools have an important role because children spend much of their time there and can learn basic information about sleep, food and exercise. Families also influence daily habits, so cooperation between school and home is likely to be more effective than relying on teachers alone.

Q3. Modern life can save time through technology, but it can also blur the boundary between work and rest. Notifications and long screen hours may make it harder to relax. The effect depends on a person's job, responsibilities and how they manage their time.

Q4. Communities can provide safe walking paths, parks, sports groups and low-cost activities. These options make exercise more accessible to people with different incomes and abilities. Campaigns can raise interest, but convenient facilities are likely to make participation easier.
F8. Culture and traditions

Q1. Traditions can connect people with their history and create a shared sense of belonging. Festivals, food and ceremonies may bring families and communities together. Their importance varies, and not everyone will relate to every tradition in the same way.

Q2. Yes, because local history can help young people understand how their communities developed and why places have particular meanings. It can also encourage respect for different experiences. Teaching it should leave room for discussion rather than presenting history as a single simple story.

Q3. Yes. A tradition can keep its central meaning while adapting its form to current needs. For example, a family celebration may use modern technology to include relatives who live abroad. Some practices may also need to change if they cause harm or exclude people.

Q4. Globalisation may introduce new music, food and ideas, which can enrich local culture. At the same time, widely marketed products can overshadow smaller traditions. Local communities can preserve what matters to them while still being open to outside influences.
F9. Shopping and consumer behaviour

Q1. Some purchases are driven by emotion, advertising or social pressure rather than real need. Buying something new can briefly improve a person's mood, and online shopping makes it easy to act on an impulse. Planning a budget and waiting before buying can help people make more considered choices.

Q2. Advertising can make products appear attractive by linking them with status, happiness or success. Repeated exposure may also make a product feel familiar. However, people do not respond to all advertising in the same way, and price, quality and personal needs still influence decisions.

Q3. Yes. Local shops can offer personal service, provide convenient access and contribute to neighbourhood life. Online shopping may offer a wider selection and easy price comparisons, so each has advantages. Many customers choose based on the product and the service they need.

Q4. People can make a shopping list, compare quality rather than only price, and pause before buying non-essential items. They can also check whether an item will be used regularly. These habits do not eliminate all impulse purchases, but they can make spending more intentional.
F10. Media and information

Q1. People follow distant events because they may affect the economy, safety, travel or issues they care about. News can also help them understand other societies. However, constant exposure to distressing stories can be overwhelming, so people may need to choose reliable sources and take breaks.

Q2. They can check who published the information, compare it with other reputable sources and look for evidence rather than relying on a headline. It is also useful to distinguish a factual report from opinion. If a claim seems surprising, checking it before sharing can prevent misinformation from spreading.

Q3. Social media allows more people to share opinions quickly and participate in public discussions. It can help important issues reach a wider audience, but it can also spread rumours or encourage hostile exchanges. The quality of discussion depends on platform design and how users behave.

Q4. Yes, because students encounter a large amount of online content. They should learn to check sources, recognise persuasive language and compare claims. These skills can help them make informed decisions beyond school, not just complete assignments.
F11. Travel and tourism

Q1. Travel gives people a chance to experience different landscapes, food and ways of life. It can also provide a break from daily routines. Some people travel for education or work rather than leisure, so motivations vary.

Q2. Tourism can create jobs and bring income to hotels, restaurants and local guides. Visitors may also support cultural sites and small businesses. The benefits are greater when local residents receive a fair share of the income and tourism is managed responsibly.

Q3. Large numbers of visitors can create congestion, litter and pressure on housing or natural areas. Popular sites may become crowded, making daily life more difficult for residents. Planning visitor numbers and investing in local infrastructure can reduce some of these problems.

Q4. Travel may become easier to plan through digital tools, and some people may choose lower-impact transport where it is practical. Costs, climate concerns and work patterns could also influence choices. The future is likely to differ between short domestic trips and long-distance travel.
F12. Artificial intelligence and the future

Q1. AI can help people complete tasks faster, organise information and automate repetitive work. Businesses may use it to improve services, while individuals may use it for translation or planning. Its usefulness depends on accuracy, privacy and whether people understand its limitations.

Q2. Tasks involving safety, empathy, ethical responsibility or complex judgement may still need strong human oversight. For example, a tool can help organise medical information, but decisions about an individual require professional judgement and context. AI can support people without taking full responsibility away from them.

Q3. Schools can teach students how to learn independently, evaluate information and use digital tools responsibly. Communication, problem-solving and adaptability will also matter because specific job tasks may change. Students need a foundation that helps them continue learning throughout their careers.

Q4. AI may replace some tasks while creating demand for other roles, but the outcome is uncertain and will vary across industries. Some workers may need retraining as jobs change. The important question is not only how many jobs appear, but whether people can access the new opportunities.
